label: Casting Motivation
notes: Open with the manufacturing question rather than the algorithm. A one-piece mold is useful only if the solid can be pulled out without colliding with any face of the mold. The chapter turns that physical clearance question into a geometric feasibility problem. The key promise is that the same low-dimensional linear programming ideas will later solve both castability tests and abstract constraint optimization.

label: Normal Test
notes: Explain the sign convention carefully. Each facet has an outward normal eta. If the removal direction d points into the forbidden side of a facet, the casting sticks. The local test d dot eta less than or equal to zero says the motion does not push into that facet. Students should read the diagram as a single face test before we intersect all face tests.

label: Direction Plane
notes: Move from directions in space to points in an affine plane. By scaling any non-horizontal removal direction to make z equal to one, each 3D facet normal induces a linear inequality in the x and y coordinates of that plane. This is the reduction that lets a casting problem become a planar half-plane feasibility problem.

label: Castability Feasibility
notes: State the orientation version of Theorem 4.2 in lecture language: for a chosen orientation of the cast, a valid removal direction exists exactly when the induced planar half-planes have a common point. The theorem is not magic; it is just the all-facets version of the previous normal test after directions have been normalized onto the plane z equals one.

label: HPI Taxonomy
notes: Use the taxonomy to build geometric vocabulary before algorithms. Intersecting half-planes can give a bounded polygon, an unbounded wedge or strip, a lower-dimensional segment or point, or nothing at all. The later algorithms must distinguish these cases because an optimization target behaves differently on each one.

label: Divide And Conquer HPI
notes: Present half-plane intersection as a convex-region merge problem. Split the constraints, recursively build two convex intersections, and then intersect those two regions. The price of the method is sorting and merge work, which gives the familiar O n log n bound when the full intersection boundary is required.

label: Sweep Merge Invariant
notes: The merge is easier to trust when its state is visible. Boundary pointers walk around two convex chains while maintaining the next candidate edge of the intersection. At each step the algorithm decides which boundary contributes the next edge and discards arcs that lie outside the other region. The invariant is that the already emitted chain is exactly the merged boundary seen so far.

label: All Solutions Cost More
notes: This slide separates two tasks students often conflate. If we need the entire feasible region, the output can have many edges and half-plane intersection naturally costs O n log n. If we only need one optimal point for a fixed-dimensional linear program, randomized incremental methods can avoid constructing the whole region and reach expected linear time.

label: LP Solution Types
notes: Classify the outcomes of a planar linear program before discussing the algorithm. The feasible set may be empty, the objective may be unbounded, or an optimum may occur along an edge or at a vertex. The vertex case is generic, but the edge case is important because it exposes degeneracy and support constraints.

label: Incremental Bounded LP
notes: Describe the incremental algorithm as a maintained certificate. After i constraints, v_i is the current optimum. If the next half-plane contains v_i, nothing changes. If it excludes v_i, the new optimum must lie on the boundary line of the violated constraint, so the repair becomes a one-dimensional linear program over that line.

label: Bad Deterministic Order
notes: Show why the same repair rule is not automatically fast. A carefully chosen deterministic order can make almost every new constraint invalidate the current optimum. Each invalidation scans earlier constraints along the new boundary, so the accumulated work forms a quadratic staircase.

label: Random Permutation
notes: The randomized algorithm uses the same geometric repair, but it removes the adversary's power to arrange constraints in the worst possible order. The plotted trace should be read qualitatively: many inserted constraints are harmless, and the expensive repair steps are sparse rather than forced at every stage.

label: Backwards Analysis
notes: Give the backwards-analysis argument in one sentence first. After i constraints are present, the optimum is determined by at most two support constraints in the plane. If we imagine deleting one random constraint from that set, the optimum changes only when a support constraint is removed, so the probability is at most two over i.

label: Unbounded Programs
notes: Unboundedness is not a failure of the model; it is a geometric outcome. If there is a feasible ray that improves the objective forever, no finite optimum exists. The tight set H star records constraints whose boundary is relevant to the direction of escape, and this lets the algorithm reason about rays rather than searching for a missing vertex.

label: Higher Dimensions
notes: Emphasize the caveat in fixed dimension. The same violated-constraint idea recurses onto a boundary hyperplane, reducing dimension by one. The constants grow with dimension, so the result is powerful for fixed low-dimensional geometry but should not be sold as a general high-dimensional linear programming method.

label: Smallest Enclosing Disks
notes: Close with the LP-type echo. The smallest enclosing disk is not a linear program, but it has the same support-set behavior: the answer is certified by at most three boundary points, and random insertion only repairs the disk when the new point lies outside. This lets students recognize the chapter's deeper pattern beyond half-planes.
